title: Verifiability, not difficulty, sets the order of automation
author: Aaron Levie

dup.label: economics credence goods an experiment on role liability verifiability reputation competition

sib.t: The Economics of Credence Goods: An Experiment on the Role of Liability, Verifiability, Reputation, and Competition

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Levie accepts the cluster’s core view that capability is task-specific and that verifiability and process redesign govern safe automation. He materially extends it by arguing that objective verifiability—not apparent difficulty—will determine automation order because it supplies both training signals and scalable operational checks, while less-verifiable knowledge work requires applied-AI systems and redesigned processes.
qs: # Verifiability, not difficulty, sets the order of automation  *Aaron Levie — X (@levie) (2026)*  We're going to be in for a strange dynamic which is that some of the "hardest" work in the world is actually prone to automation first, particularly due to its verifiability.

The implications of this distinction are that -even as model capability continues to increase exponentially- there will be a lot done at the applied AI layer than just the the model itself, and much of the processes themselves will even need to change over time to get the full gains from automation.

kp.k: Verifiability may make difficult work automate first
kp.d: Aaron Levie predicts that some exceptionally difficult, high-value work may be automated before other work because its correctness can be objectively tested. He identifies mathematics, cybersecurity and coding as examples. This is a prospective argument about the order of automation, not an empirical finding or a dated implementation forecast.
qs: We're going to be in for a strange dynamic which is that some of the "hardest" work in the world is actually prone to automation first, particularly due to its verifiability.
Math, cyber, and code -while being insanely hard and high value fields- have the benefit of being able to be tested that it's correct objectively.

kp.k: Objective testing benefits both training and deployment
kp.d: Levie identifies two mechanisms linking verifiability to automation: objectively testable tasks provide clearer reward signals during model training, and their outputs can be tested at scale during deployment. His argument concerns scalable testing of correctness rather than human checking of legal output.
qs: This has two immediate benefits: the training of the models offers clearer reward signals, and then the running of the models allows you to know that it's working properly because you can test the results in a scalable way.

kp.k: Client acceptance of legal clauses lacks instant verifiability
kp.d: Levie contrasts objectively testable work with deciding which legal clauses a client will accept, alongside marketing, sales and business budgeting decisions. He argues that these tasks depend on changing circumstances, operator opinions and risk levels, and the right input context; they lack a single correct answer, and the suitability of an answer may only become knowable much later. The legal example concerns client agreement, not the correctness of legal research or citations.
qs: Conversely, in other domains of work, there's much less instant verifiability.

Which legal clauses your client will agree to, what marketing campaign to run with based on changing sentiment, which message your sales prospect will want to hear, what financial targets and budget to set for a business, and so on.

All of these domains have changing internal and external factors, they don't have "one right answer", they rely on the opinions and risk levels of the operators, they're highly sensitive to getting the right input context first, and in many cases the right answer can't even be known for quite some time after the model generates the results.

kp.k: Automation gains require application and process changes
kp.d: Levie argues that increasing model capability alone will not deliver the full gains from automation: substantial work will remain at the applied AI layer, and processes will need to change over time. He further speculates that knowledge work may require new testing capabilities analogous to those available for software. Neither the process changes nor the proposed capabilities are specified in detail.
qs: The implications of this distinction are that -even as model capability continues to increase exponentially- there will be a lot done at the applied AI layer than just the the model itself, and much of the processes themselves will even need to change over time to get the full gains from automation.
We may even need all new capabilities to be able to "test" knowledge work over time as we have had with software.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Aaron Levie predicts that objective verifiability, rather than difficulty alone, will influence which work is automated first; less readily testable knowledge work will require changes beyond improvements to models.
pts.d: Levie argues that difficult, high-value work in mathematics, cybersecurity and coding is particularly amenable to early automation because objective testing supplies clearer training rewards and scalable checks on outputs. In contrast, he identifies predicting which legal clauses a client will accept, along with marketing, sales and business budgeting decisions, as work without immediately verifiable, uniquely correct answers. He predicts substantial work at the applied-AI layer and changes to work processes to realise automation gains, and suggests that new ways to test knowledge work may be needed. His legal example concerns client acceptance of clauses, not a claim that all legal work is unverifiable or that lawyers will be replaced.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Levie offers a conceptual mechanism and illustrative task comparisons, rather than empirical evidence.
pts.d: The proposed mechanism is that testable correctness improves both model training signals and the ability to check results at scale. His contrasting examples depend on preferences, risk tolerance, contextual information and delayed outcomes. The document provides no quantitative data, benchmarks, case studies, cited research or documented experience demonstrating the predicted automation order. The statement that model capability continues to increase exponentially is asserted without supporting measurements.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The prediction is forward-looking from the source's 2026 publication context, with no dated automation milestones.
pts.d: Levie predicts a relative order of automation rather than a timetable. Earlier automation is conditional on outputs being objectively testable and checks being scalable. For less verifiable work, progress depends on obtaining appropriate context, accommodating changing circumstances and operator preferences, and potentially waiting for outcomes to become observable. Process adaptation is expected over time even with continued model capability growth. New testing capabilities are presented as a possibility, not a certainty.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claim concerns technical and knowledge-work domains broadly, including legal professionals working with client preferences and organisations implementing AI.
pts.d: Mathematics, cybersecurity and coding are identified as domains susceptible to earlier automation despite their difficulty and value. People selecting legal clauses, marketing campaigns, sales messages and financial targets face less immediate feedback about whether AI-generated answers are suitable. In the legal example, client willingness to accept clauses makes preferences and risk tolerance consequential. Developers and organisations applying AI are implicitly affected by the predicted need for application-layer development, process redesign and new testing methods. Levie does not identify particular law-firm segments, staffing effects, pricing changes or access-to-justice outcomes.
